title.en: US-China AI rivalry heats up as Chinese models gain ground
title.zh: 中美人工智能竞争加剧，中国模型迎头赶上

summary.en: China's AI platforms are rapidly advancing, narrowing the gap with US technology. This progress has led to renewed threats from the Trump administration, alongside accusations of intellectual property theft, raising concerns about escalating tensions between the two nations.
summary.zh: 中国的人工智能平台正迅速缩小与美国同行的差距。这一进展引发了特朗普政府新的威胁，并伴随着知识产权盗窃的指控，令人担忧两国之间的紧张关系可能升级。

body.en:
China's AI platforms are rapidly closing the gap with their US counterparts, prompting fresh threats from the Trump administration. With accusations of intellectual property theft, could tensions boil over?

In what seems like the blink of an eye,  China has gone from being up to five years behind the United States in top-tier artificial intelligence (AI) to lagging by just a few months.

While US players, including Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's ChatGPT , have spent hundreds of billions of dollars to push the frontier of AI, China has pursued a very different path .

Faced with US curbs on high-end chips that help AI to do its most advanced thinking, Chinese tech firms have prioritized dozens of open-source AI models built on "good enough"  technology .

These platforms, including DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen and Xiaomi's MiMo, are now widely deployed across Chinese businesses, government services and consumer devices.

In the latest sign of the gap closing, Chinese startup Moonshot AI last week unveiled Kimi K3, a model that rivals one of the most advanced AI models — Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 — on key benchmarks.

In some tests, Kimi K3 matches or even surpasses Claude with far less computing power and at a fraction of the cost. 

Global technology specialist Alvin W. Graylin thinks Kimi K3's arrival turns high-end AI from an expensive luxury into something practical and affordable.

"For 98% of customers, the 1 to 2% difference [in knowledge] isn't worth paying 10 to 20 times more."

China's latest advance has already drawn a strong reaction from Washington, with US President Donald Trump now threatening to block US access to Chinese AI models.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, meanwhile, warned earlier this week that the US could sanction Chinese models over alleged intellectual property (IP) theft.

Anthropic  and OpenAI have accused Chinese labs of using their models to train their own systems, a process known as distilling.

While distilling is a common practice by AI labs worldwide to a limited extent, the companies say their models have been bombarded with queries to harvest advanced reasoning. The White House warned in April that China was doing it on an "industrial scale."

Beijing has hit back, rejecting the accusations as baseless and calling US threats of sanctions and model bans "technological bullying" to contain China's rise.

Giulia Neaher, a research analyst at the Strategic Foresight Hub at the Washington-based Stimson Center think tank, downplayed the role of distilling in Kimi's progress.

"A great degree [of its success] is due to the talent, infrastructure and the resources that were poured into building this...
body.zh: 中国的人工智能平台正在迅速缩小与美国同行的差距，引发了特朗普政府的新威胁。随着知识产权盗窃的指控，紧张局势会升级吗？ 似乎一眨眼的功夫，中国在顶级人工智能 (AI) 领域就从落后美国五年变为仅落后几个月。 尽管包括 Anthropic 的 Claude 和 OpenAI 的 ChatGPT 在内的美国企业已经花费了数千亿美元来推动人工智能的前沿发展，但中国却走了一条截然不同的道路。 面对美国对帮助人工智能实现最先进思维的高端芯片的限制，中国科技公司优先考虑了数十种基于“足够好”技术的开源人工智能模型。 这些平台，包括 DeepSeek、阿里巴巴的 Qwen 和小米的 MiMo，现已广泛部署在中国企业、政府服务和消费设备中。 作为缩小差距的最新迹象，中国初创公司 Moonshot AI 上周推出了 Kimi K3，该模型在关键基准测试上可与最先进的人工智能模型之一——Anthropic 的 Claude Fable 5 相媲美。 在某些测试中，Kimi K3 可以与 Claude 相媲美甚至超过 Claude，但其计算能力却要低得多，而成本却只是 Claude 的一小部分。 全球技术专家 Alvin W. Graylin 认为 Kimi K3 的到来将高端人工智能从昂贵的奢侈品变成了实用且负担得起的东西。 “对于 98% 的客户来说，[知识] 1% 到 2% 的差异并不值得多付 10 到 20 倍的费用。” 中国的最新进展已经引起华盛顿的强烈反应，美国总统唐纳德·特朗普现在威胁要阻止美国使用中国的人工智能模型。 与此同时，财政部长斯科特·贝森特本周早些时候警告称，美国可能会因涉嫌盗窃知识产权而制裁中国模型。 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 指责中国实验室使用他们的模型来训练他们自己的系统，这一过程被称为蒸馏。 虽然提炼是全球人工智能实验室在一定程度上的常见做法，但这些公司表示，他们的模型已经受到查询的轰炸，以收获高级推理。白宫四月份警告说，中国正在以“工业规模”这样做。 北京方面予以反击，否认这些指控毫无根据，并称美国威胁实施制裁和示范禁令是“技术欺凌”，旨在遏制中国的崛起。 华盛顿智库史汀生中心战略远见中心的研究分析师朱莉娅·尼赫（Giulia Neaher）淡化了提炼在基米进步中的作用。 “[其成功]很大程度上归功于为建设这个项目而投入的人才、基础设施和资源......

reflection.en: In a world of intense technological competition and rising international tensions, the call to live peaceably with all people becomes profoundly relevant. Even amidst accusations and threats, seeking paths to de-escalation and mutual respect is vital for global stability. Yahweh's wisdom encourages us to pursue peace wherever possible, even when faced with...

title.en: Australia news live: NSW police charge woman with 62 counts over alleged threatening letters to politicians, media and place of worship

summary.en: New South Wales police have charged a woman with 62 counts related to alleged threatening letters sent to politicians, media organizations, and a place of worship.
summary.zh: 新南威尔士州警方已对一名女子提出62项指控，涉及据称寄给政界人士、媒体机构和一处礼拜场所的恐吓信件。

body.en:
A Sydney woman has been charged with 62 offences after allegedly sending threatening letters to organisations and individuals, including politicians, a place of worship and a media outlet.

This follows the investigation by a newly formed strike force established in response to “a large volume of letters” sent to several individuals and organisations.

Officers searched a home in Constitution Hill last month, seizing electronic devices before arresting the 36-year-old woman on Wednesday.

The charges include sending letters containing threats of death or grievous bodily harm, stalking and intimidation, and dishonestly obtaining financial advantage by deception.
body.zh: 一名悉尼女子因涉嫌向政治家、礼拜场所和媒体等组织和个人发送威胁信而被指控犯有 62 项罪行。 此前，一支新成立的打击部队针对发给多个个人和组织的“大量信件”而成立，并对此进行了调查。 警察上个月搜查了宪法山的一处住宅，没收了电子设备，然后于周三逮捕了这名 36 岁的女子。 这些指控包括发送包含死亡或严重身体伤害威胁的信件、跟踪和恐吓，以及通过欺骗不诚实地获取经济利益。

reflection.en: This news reminds us of the profound impact words can have, as reckless speech can pierce like a sword, causing fear and distress. In a world where communication can easily turn hostile, Yahweh calls us to use our words for healing and peace, rather than for harm.
reflection.zh: 这则新闻提醒我们言语的深远影响，因为鲁莽的言语能像刀剑一样刺伤人，造成恐惧和不安。在一个沟通很容易变得充满敌意的世界里，雅伟呼召我们用言语带来医治与和平，而非伤害。

verse.textEn: The words of the reckless pierce like swords, but the tongue of the wise brings healing.
verse.textZh: 说话浮躁的，如刀刺人；智慧人的舌头却为医人的良药。

body.en:
Kmart recently launched a new accessory — dubbed Camera Glasses — which it said blends stylish eyewear with built-in camera technology.

At a glance, the black-framed spectacles from Kmart's in-house brand Anko look like any ordinary pair of glasses. But by Monday 3 August, there were reports the product was sold out online.

At $89, the glasses provide a low-cost alternative to the smart glasses designed by glasses company Ray-Ban and Facebook owners Meta, which start at $337. The latest generation of this technology costs more than $700.

A recent promotional video for Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses, featuring celebrity Kylie Jenner, showcased its features. Those include an ultra-HD camera, discreet open-ear Bluetooth speakers, and translation technology.

In July, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said people who don't wear smart glasses in the future will be at a "pretty significant cognitive disadvantage".

There are similar products available or in development by the companies Samsung, Rokid, Even Realities, Solos and XREAL.

Milica Stilinovic is a postdoctoral research associate for the Governing Immersive Tech Project at the University of Sydney. She told SBS News that "a lot of flak has been driven towards Meta currently because they are market leaders".

But she said: "If the price is cheaper ... if you're not paying at the bridge, you may pay at the toll.

"We still need to ask ourselves, this data that we're essentially generating for these companies; how is it being handled, by whom and at what cost?"

Stilinovic also said wearable technology, regardless of its price point, raises complex questions around privacy and security.

Depending on the product, they may have AI-enabled programs embedded, which analyse human behaviours including eye movements, head tracking and voice patterns.

"They are picking up data of where you're walking around, the space that you're in, what you're doing at particular times ... even to the extent of knowing the map out of your home," Stilinovic said.

Facial recognition technology is not active in most smart glasses on the market.

However, in 2024, students from Harvard University combined smart glasses, facial search engines, AI language tools and public databases to test surveillance capabilities. They found information including a person's home address, name and phone number — just by looking at them.

Fareed Kaviani is a research fellow at the Emerging Technologies Research Lab at Monash University. In 2024, he co-authored a paper examining social perceptions of smart glasses use in Australia.

body.en:
While most Australians in Europe are at the beach, NSW aerial firefighting pilot Alex Pay spends his long summer days at a Greek airbase, waiting for a call to action.

"When you get a fire call, you're gonna be airborne in 15 minutes," he told SBS News.

Once in the air, Pay can spend up to 10 hours supporting local authorities in Greece's fight against wildfires, which over the past week saw two pilots killed and hundreds of thousands forced to evacuate.

Pay, 31, works for a small but growing number of Australian private aerial firefighting companies based in Western Europe during this year's fire season, which is shaping up to be the continent's worst in record.

It also comes as Australia's own looming El Niño threatens to turn up the heat on our own summer bushfire risk .

Pay is a third-generation pilot with Pay's Air Service, which is based in the NSW Hunter Region.

"I remember as a kid flying with my dad to visit my grandparents," he told SBS News.

He pilots one of 14 aircraft his company has based throughout Greece for the summer. It’s his second season in the country, and the fifth overall for his company.

They fly a variant of the Air Tractor AT-802, nicknamed the "Fire Boss" — an amphibious aircraft that scoops water into a tank, or "hopper", controlled by a computerised fire gate that can be adjusted to match exact conditions.

In Australia, there were around 130 certified firefighting aeroplane operators or individual pilots, with a further 186 helicopter operators in 2021, according to Australia's Civil Aviation Authority.

Andrew Mackay is from Ballarat-based Field Air Group, which also has planes stationed in Greece this summer supporting Pay's.

"We like to say in our industry that it's not the aircraft that put out the fires, it's the ground crew — we're merely a tool to assist them," he told SBS News.

He said pilots will often work on either side of the fire to create a "triangle or an arrowhead, so the fire comes to a point where the ground crew can then extinguish that".

Sometimes they will drop water or retardant directly onto a house under threat from a blaze.

"We spent a lot of time training and preparing scenarios that give us a good education on what we might see on the fire ground," Pay said.

On Sunday, a Greek and a Danish national were killed after two helicopters collided while fighting a fire west of Athens.

The helicopters were leased from Australian company McDermott Aviation, which said in a statement it was "deeply saddened" by the tragedy.

title.en: Jetstar’s new overhead baggage rules explained: When they start and what you'll pay
title.zh: 捷星航空新随身行李规定解读：何时生效，费用几何

summary.en: Budget airline Jetstar is changing its carry-on baggage policy, moving from a weight-based limit to a new model based on size. This adjustment will affect when the new rules start and what passengers will be charged.
summary.zh: 廉价航空公司捷星航空将更改其随身行李政策，从基于重量的限制转向基于尺寸的新模式。这项调整将影响新规何时生效以及乘客需要支付的费用。

body.en:
Storing carry-on baggage in overhead lockers on Jetstar flights will cost up to $52 one-way, as the budget airline announces new charges for passengers.

Jetstar chief executive Stephanie Tully says the changes to the airline's carry-on baggage allowances will streamline boarding and help more flights depart on time.

"Our new carry-on baggage model provides more choice to customers while helping to keep our fares low," Tully added.

"You only pay for what you need — travelling with less means paying less, and you can always add more if you need."

The changes follow "extensive research and feedback from customers and crew" which found frustrations with weighing bags and finding enough room in overhead lockers, Jetstar said.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

From 2 February, Jetstar will lift its 7kg carry-on weight limit in favour of a size-based carry-on baggage model.

Cabin baggage scales used to weigh passengers' carry-on bags before boarding will no longer be "routinely" used, the airline said.

Passengers will be able to bring one small bag to place under the seat, such as a backpack, handbag or laptop bag. That bag can weigh up to 10kg and be up to 40 x 30 x 20cm. Any bags larger than that will incur a fee.

Passengers who want to store a larger carry-on bag in overhead lockers will be charged between $25 and $52 one-way, depending on the flight route, for "limited" priority carry-on.

Jetstar said the fee for a one-way flight from Launceston to Sydney would start at $25, rising to $33 for a one-way flight between Sydney and Melbourne and $52 for a one-way flight between Cairns and Tokyo.

Priority boarding will be provided for passengers who pay for the carry-on option.

If you're travelling with an infant, you can bring an extra under-the-seat bag at no extra cost.

body.en:
Ruby and her 11-year-old son Mark were dreading the day his scores on the national school assessment program were released.

And they confirmed the family's worst fears: despite working hard to learn, the Year 5 student remained behind his peers.

Mark, whose name the Australian Associated Press agreed not to publish, was one of more than 1.3 million children in Years 3, 5, 7, and 9 who sat the National Assessment Program — Literacy and Numeracy (NAPLAN) in 2026.

As the only standardised national assessment, NAPLAN was primarily designed to help governments and schools measure results and fix funding or teaching shortfalls.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

"When I got the results, because it comes under Mark's name, he wanted to see his results,'' Ruby said.

"I just thought to myself, 'How could it be right at the bottom when he's improved so much?'"

But scores for reading were worse than in 2025 for every year level, and Year 5 students were the only cohort whose writing ability had improved.

Overall, about one in three students across all levels did not meet basic literacy and numeracy benchmarks, falling into "developing" and "needs additional support" categories.

The writing scores were a particular concern in the two lowest grades tested, with less than 10 per cent of students exceeding national benchmarks.

Numeracy results had improved for most cohorts since 2025, though Year 3's score had decreased.

Results from previous years showed a clear literacy divide between children from wealthy, educated areas and those who grow up in areas of low socio-economic status.

Ruby said she also struggled at school and her challenges went unnoticed because of her learning environment.

"With Mark, I just wish there was more people, just more at the school to help," she said.

Better support that understands the specific needs of struggling families would help improve results, The Smith Family chief executive Doug Taylor said.

"With 72,000 low-income students across Australia, the right support at the right time can make a huge difference," he said, noting schools should also consider the skills students had beyond academic ones.

In rural communities and towns with high Indigenous populations, results have dramatically improved in recent years.

That was due to increased funding and the use of explicit teaching models, Education Minister Jason Clare said in a speech at the Garma Indigenous festival over the weekend.

"Over the last four years, the numeracy results of Indigenous students have gone up and up,'' he said.

title.en: 2026 Census: The new questions on gender and sexual orientation explained
title.zh: 2026 年人口普查：关于性别和性取向的新问题得到解释

summary.en: Gender identity, sexuality and ancestry: Here's what's new in the 2026 Census.
summary.zh: 这是一则来自澳洲栏目的新闻，重点涉及和平与克制。如需完整细节，请阅读英文原始报道。

body.en:
The Census of Population and Housing has long tracked a changing Australia — but for more than a century, a piece of the nation's story has been missing, LGBTIQ+ Health Australia CEO Nicky Bath says.

Bath says the organisation has been calling for the addition of questions regarding sexual orientation, gender identification and expression.

"I remember in the run-up to the 2021 Census being contacted by older people who thought that they wouldn't be alive for the 2026 Census, and it was very sad for them that they wouldn't be able to participate ... in this way," she told SBS News.

The 2026 Census will now include two new questions about gender and sexual orientation.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

Respondents will still be asked about their sex recorded at birth, but people over the age of 16 can also specify their gender as male, female, non-binary or another term.

An optional question regarding sexual orientation has been added, with answers including straight, gay or lesbian, bisexual or an open-ended response for another term.

Bath said Census data — which will be released in three phases starting from June 2027 — will inform the availability, funding and location of LGBTQI+ community and health services.

"The decision has been a long time coming ... for many people, being able to mark those boxes in the Census is really important with regards to validation and for us to be seen as important members of the community. That's a really important historical moment."

Advocates like Equality Australia say the number of people living in houseboats has been recorded in the Census for decades, but LGBTQI+ populations have not been traced.

Anna Brown, CEO of Equality Australia, said Census data collected about LGBTQI+ people would be "transformative".

"We're really looking forward to learning just how many LGBTQ+ people there are in Australia, because we know that if we aren't counted, we remain invisible in the data that shapes decisions about our lives," she told SBS News.

"Better data leads to better decisions on health, housing, education, aged care, and community services. Until now, governments have been making these decisions without a complete picture of our communities."

Brown has also called for Australians with innate variations of sex characteristics or intersex people to be counted by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

"We will continue to advocate for its inclusion and work with the ABS ... towards recommending that this population be included," she said.

Census questions are informed by the 2020 ABS standards for sex, gender, variations in sex characteristics, and sexual orientation variables....

title.en: Australians seeing record gains and losses, as 'cracks' in housing market appear

summary.en: Experts report a widening gap in property prices across Australia, with some homeowners experiencing significant gains while others face substantial losses, indicating emerging vulnerabilities in the housing market.

body.en:
Property prices in Australia consistently reach record highs, but a "first crack in profitability" could signal a market downturn.

In the first half of 2026, 97.4 per cent of house resales resulted in a profit, slightly down from 97.5 per cent 12 months prior, according to new data from Domain released on Wednesday.

While it is a modest decline of just 0.1 per cent, it may indicate that the extended period of strong resale profitability is beginning to taper off.

Most people selling properties will still make "substantial gains", Domains chief residential economist Nicola Powell told SBS News.

However, the slight fall in national profitability suggests a slowing property market that could see prices fall in the future.

"While that shift is small, I think it is significant because what it's telling us is that resale profitability is a lagging indicator and tends to follow changes in home pricing," she explained.

"We've got some of our capital cities now going backward in price and particularly in some of our markets, we are seeing an increase in loss-making resales."

REA Group Senior Economic Analyst Megan Lieu said realestate.com.au data also revealed a drop in profitability.

In the past six months to July, 94.4 per cent of home resales made a profit, down from 94.9 per cent in the previous six months to January, she said.

But while properties are seeing larger average losses as profitability declines, some markets are soaring.

While slightly fewer properties are making a profit compared to 12 months ago, successful sellers are still enjoying record returns.

Median resale profits climbed to record levels of $458,000 for houses and $237,000 for units nationally.

Sydney posted the country’s largest resale returns, with the median house vendor achieving a profit of $739,500.

Meanwhile, Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide are increasingly standing out as the strongest markets for seller returns, with almost every resale delivering a gain.

Perth recorded the greatest proportion of profitable house resales, with 99.6 per cent of sellers making a profit on their transaction. Brisbane led the unit market, where 99.5 per cent of resales generated a positive return.

In contrast, Melbourne remained the weakest capital city market for units. More than one in four sellers sold for less than their original purchase price, while Melbourne also recorded one of the highest shares of loss-making house resales, alongside Canberra.

Surprisingly, some areas saw both record profitability gains and losses over the year.

An arson attack on a Melbourne defence firm is now being investigated as an act of terrorism, with counter-terror police alleging the offenders had pro-Palestinian motives.

On 5 July, machining manufacturer Lovitt Technologies was attacked in the early hours of the morning by arsonists who set three vehicles alight and graffitied a building.

The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism team (JCTT), spanning Australian Federal Police (AFP), Victoria Police and ASIO, has released images of the alleged vandals, probing whether "far-left activists with anarchist and revolutionary ideologies" orchestrated the incident.

The group is alleged to have targeted the company because of its links with the defence force supply chain, claiming responsibility in an online video and advising on how to carry out similar attacks.

The JCTT said the alleged offenders "outlined a number of grievances in support of Palestine" and were accused of targeting the company because they believed it was part of a broader Australian Defence Force supply chain.

The JCCT has confirmed to SBS News that the terror investigation, known as Operation Braehead, is the first to specifically target pro-Palestinian activism in Australia since the October 7 attacks. The charges carry a life sentence as a maximum penalty.

"We cannot overstate the seriousness of this criminality and the AFP, together with our partners, will not tolerate acts of terror motivated by extremist ideologies aiming to cause fear and anguish in our community," AFP detective superintendent Anthony Hall said in a statement.

"At any time, we could be knocking on the door of the accused group. We know this is making some in the group anxious — and it should, because we are determined to bring them before the courts."

body.en:
It was once a dream of many: work hard and retire in your 60s. Now, more Australians are employed into their 70s, 80s and even 90s. Insight meets those still working by choice, those who can't afford to stop, and asks what happens when you keep working later in life? Watch Insight episode Working Later in Life on SBS On Demand.

Working Later In Life episode • Insight • News And Current Affairs • 52m I was devastated when I turned 65.

I was working as an interpreter for a government telephone interpreter service, and at the time, 65 was the compulsory retirement age from the public service.

My body and mind felt young — I was perfectly capable of work — and people needed my help. I couldn't believe that an arbitrary age meant I had to stop working full-time.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

I went to the union and to a solicitor, but they couldn't help me, so I had to retire — kicking and screaming on my way out. But I found a workaround: freelance work.

I'm now 94 years old, interpreting and translating in both the private and public sectors (including Centrelink), and have no plans to retire soon.

Becoming an interpreter was always a natural progression for me; I speak a few languages, and I love dealing with people.

I was born and raised for the first 12 years of my life in Hungary. But in 1945, near the end of World War Two, my parents and I fled as refugees to Germany after the Soviet Red Army invaded and occupied our country.

I already knew Hungarian, but I learnt German, English, Latin and French through my six years of schooling in Germany, which have been very helpful to know.

I arrived in Melbourne with my family in January 1951, after 65 days of travel, as displaced persons from the war.

I was 18 years old and still remember feeling a heat I had never experienced in my life when we were taken to Bonegilla, an ex-army camp near Albury in northern Victoria that was then used as a camp to process post-war European migrants.

Because the camp was full, we were put in an army tent — and that is how I started my life in Australia.

It wasn't until the late 1950s, when I was in my late 20s, a mother and working an admin role, that my interpreting career began.

The 1956 Hungarian Revolution brought a wave of Hungarian migrants to Australia in the years that followed. But there was no community interpreter service here at the time, and people needed help.

So I stepped forward as an interpreter. I believe it's important to be understood as a person — to say what you want to say and be able to express yourself. And if you don't speak the language of a place, that's very hard to do.

verse.textEn: Yahweh detests dishonest scales, but accurate weights find favor with him.
verse.textZh: 诡诈的天平为雅伟所憎恶；公平的法码为他所喜悦。

title.en: Aboriginal police officers in the NT underpaid and racially abused, a new class action alleges
title.zh: 一项新的集体诉讼称，北领地的原住民警察工资过低并受到种族虐待

summary.en: Aboriginal community police officers in the NT Police Force allege they were subject to racial discrimination while serving.
summary.zh: 这是一则来自澳洲栏目的新闻，重点涉及公义、尊严与问责。如需完整细节，请阅读英文原始报道。

body.en:
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this story includes the name of an Indigenous person who has passed away.

When former AFL player for Essendon, Shawn Lewfatt, signed up as an Aboriginal Community Police Officer in Darwin in 1998, he was excited by the chance to work with his own people "for the better".

Now, he says, he would "never encourage" his adult children to join the Northern Territory Police Force (NTPF).

"My aim is that hopefully one day I can turn to young people and encourage them to join," he told SBS News.

Lewfatt is part of a landmark class action filed in the Federal Court against the NTPF seeking compensation for allegations of racial discrimination and racial vilification while serving as Aboriginal Community Police Officers (ACPOS) going back almost three decades.

"Our clients allege they were underpaid, provided fewer opportunities for career advancement and subjected to persistent racist conduct while serving communities across the NT," Seb O'Meara of Gordon Legal, who is representing the ACPOs in the class action, told SBS News.

The class action, run on behalf of all present and former Aboriginal police officers in the NT Police, seeks to speed up reform following the 2019 police shooting of Kumanjayi Walker and the subsequent inquest, which shone the spotlight on systemic racism within the NT Police Force.

A spokesperson for the NTPF told SBS News they were aware of ongoing legal proceedings, and it would be inappropriate to comment further.

Despite growing up in Darwin, Lewfatt told SBS News that when he walked through the doors of the police station, he felt like a "foreigner in my hometown".

"I felt immediately weird in the way they would speak about Aboriginal people, and it became clear to me that it was the norm."

Lewfett, who remains on the Force on leave, alleged he witnessed "unlawful assaults on Indigenous people", including one incident involving a non-Aboriginal police officer urinating into a wine cask belonging to an Aboriginal member of the public who had stashed it in a public toilet.

Lewfatt said that racism in the force is embedded in the culture, rather than in individuals.

"It's the systematic racism where there are a lot of good people who may not be racist but do not call out racism either when they come across it."

Lewfatt's first complaint was made public in September 2024, when The Australian newspaper reported details of a complaint made by him and at least 20 serving Aboriginal police officers to the Australian Human Rights Commission alleging racial discrimination and unequal pay for Aboriginal Community Police...

reflection.en: This story draws attention to justice, dignity, and accountability. Micah 6:8 reminds us to meet sharp headlines with justice tempered by mercy, asking how faithful people can respond with wisdom instead of noise.
